The one that matters most is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, *Conservation Science and Practice*).

Why it stands out for the project:

- **It is the proof-of-concept your project is trying to build.** In January 2024, forecasts ahead of the 2023/24 El Niño flagged a high risk of marine heatwaves in Australia. Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Here's what I found, in three parts.

---

## 1. Best-fitting open grant

**#1 — "Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate"** (Horizon CL5-2027-01-D1-07, €3M–€15M, deadline **4 March 2027**, still open).

This is the strongest match for the Marine heatwave early warning project (#11) for a concrete reason: the call explicitly asks for AI-based approaches, a hierarchy of models, and seamless prediction from short-term to sub-seasonal scales to improve early warning for extreme events. That is almost word-for-word what #11 does — marine heatwave prediction using ML and data assimilation, with subseasonal forecasting and sea surface temperature as core concepts. The call also encourages integration with Copernicus and Destination Earth, which gives a natural operationalisation angle for an early-warning system.

The biggest doubt: the call is broad (any extreme event, continental to local scale), so a proposal would need to be framed tightly around marine heatwaves to stand out, and it expects a consortium with multiple lines of evidence (high-res Earth system models, retrospective analyses, case studies). That's a bigger ask than the project's current three-person team.

The other open grants on the project's slate are weaker fits:
- **#5** (Global Ocean Observing System, €50M, deadline 16 Feb 2027) is about observation infrastructure and governance, not prediction.
- **#2** (Antarctica/Southern Ocean, deadline 23 Sep 2027) is regionally specific and cryosphere-focused.
- **#7** (Disaster decision support, deadline 4 Nov 2027) is about civil-protection systems, not climate science.
- **#19** (NSF OTIC) is instrumentation development.
- **#20** (Carbon sources/sinks) and **#21** (Biodiversity data integration) are different scientific questions.

---

## 2. Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and the requirement-slot analysis point to two people:

- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#18)** — declared interests in circulation and turbulence and physics-informed ML. He covers the "Earth system models" slot (declared: regional ocean models). His work on fast, physics-informed surrogates for ocean models maps directly onto the call's ask for improved prediction and projection modelling. He is a member of #11.

- **You, Mara (#14)** — declared interests in data assimilation with ML and ocean extremes. The ranking notes that the lab's specific focus on forecasting marine heatwaves using ML and data assimilation directly addresses the call's problem. You are the PI and a member of #11.

**Gaps no one in the lab covers:** extreme events in a changing climate (as a formal research area), digital twins, Copernicus integration, and Destination Earth. These would need to be filled by partners.

My read: **Tomás should lead the scientific core** (model hierarchy, physics-informed surrogates, prediction skill) and **you should lead the overall proposal** as PI, framing the marine heatwave early-warning application and the data-assimilation pipeline. That splits the two strongest declared strengths and keeps the project's own members at the centre.

---

## 3. Who outside the lab could partner

Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I can only tell you what the call itself suggests and what the gaps imply:

- **Copernicus Marine Service / ECMWF** — the call explicitly encourages integration with Copernicus and Destination Earth. A partner who can speak to operational SST forecasting and the Copernicus Marine Service would fill the "Copernicus" gap and give the proposal an operational-uptake story.
- **A high-resolution Earth system modelling group** — the call expects a "hierarchy of models" including high-res ESMs. No one in the lab declares ESM work, so a partner with that capability (e.g. a national meteorological service or a university climate-modelling group) would fill that gap.
- **A digital-twin or AI-for-climate group** — the call names digital twins specifically. No one in the lab declares this.
- **A low- to middle-income country partner** — the call encourages international cooperation with LMICs for capacity building, which is a plus for the proposal's score.

I could not run a co-authorship search to name specific people, so these are role descriptions rather than names. If you turn on collaborator search, I can look for specific researchers who match those gaps.

---

**One caveat:** I could not read the full project record for #11 (the call was denied), so I worked from the project's declared concepts, its members, and the grant text. If the project has a more detailed problem statement or milestones that I'm not seeing, the fit assessment could shift.

Here's what I found. I'll walk through the best-fit call, who should lead, and the partnership question.

## Best fit: #20 Green, circular and resilient harbours

Of the open calls I checked, this is the closest to the Plastic pathways project (#2). It's a Horizon Europe call under the Mission "Restore our Ocean and Waters" (€1M–€8.9M, deadline 2027-09-21) that asks for place-based, people-centred actions to reduce pollution and environmental degradation in ports across four sea basins. The strongest reason it fits: the project's core problem — tracking and mitigating marine plastic pollution in coastal waters — is exactly the kind of pollution-reduction action this call funds, and the project's satellite remote sensing and Lagrangian tracking methods are directly usable for monitoring pollution in harbour areas. The biggest doubt: the call requires demonstration in at least 4 ports with strong involvement of port authorities and public administrations, which is a consortium-building requirement the project hasn't addressed yet.

The other open calls I checked are further from the project's core:
- #19 (Microplastics Research and Resource Coordination Center, deadline 2026-12-01) is a US NIEHS U24 coordination center focused on health effects and analytical standardization of micro/nanoplastics — a biomedical framing, not an ocean pathways one.
- #9 (ZEWT, deadline 2027-04-14) is about pollution from waterborne transport and zero-carbon fuels, not plastic pathways per se.
- #5 (biotech recycling of complex plastics, deadline 2027-09-22) is a materials-science call about recycling technologies, not environmental tracking.
- #25 (remote sensing + in-situ biodiversity data integration, deadline 2027-09-22) and #27 (Global Ocean Observing System, deadline 2027-02-16) are observation-infrastructure calls that overlap with the lab's methods but not with the plastic-pathways problem.

## Who in the lab should lead

The project's three members are Jonah Whitcombe (#15), Priya Raman (#16), and you (#14).

- **Jonah** is the natural lead. He declares marine litter and Lagrangian analysis in his profile, which are the two concepts the project itself declares. He's the only member whose declared interests sit directly on the project's problem.
- **Priya** is the strongest technical partner for the application: she declares satellite ocean remote sensing and coastal water quality, and the nightly ranking notes her deep-learning work on satellite ocean colour for mapping harmful algal blooms as directly supporting the remote-sensing monitoring the call asks for.
- **You** are the closest third match, with your data-assimilation and ocean-extremes background supporting the forecasting and data-integration parts of the proposal.

One gap to flag: the project declares two concepts — floating debris detection and Lagrangian particle tracking — that none of its members declares in their profile. If Jonah's Lagrangian work is the basis for that, it may be worth updating his profile so the application's evidence is visible to Mylo.

## Who outside the lab could partner

I can't name specific people outside the lab: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I have no consented external profiles to draw from. What I can say is what the call requires of the consortium, so you know what to look for:

- **Port authorities and public administrations** in at least four ports, one in each of the four basins (Atlantic/Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic/North Sea, Danube including Black Sea). The call strongly encourages these as partners.
- **Local and regional stakeholders** in the port communities.
- **Industry partners** relevant to the pollution-reduction solutions you'd propose.

If you'd like, I can help you think through which basins and port types would be most natural for the project's methods, or draft the consortium structure for the application.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.

   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus the papers and a funding angle.

## Where the project stands

The project is a lab-scoped effort with three members: Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. I have to be upfront: the project record I can see holds only the name, scope and membership — no confirmed problem statement, method, stage, milestones or open blockers are on file. So I can't tell you how far along the work is or what's blocking it; if the team has confirmed a state in the app, it isn't visible to me here.

What I can say is that the project's slate has been active since 2026-11-10, with several items flagged as new this week (2026-11-13). The slate skews toward marine-litter tracking, ocean forecasting and satellite remote sensing, which matches the lab's declared "Debris pathways" cluster.

## Three most relevant new papers

1. **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-point item: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, with scripts and aggregated results, validated against field records using ROMS flow fields. This is essentially a ready-made method and codebase for tracking where floating debris ends up — the core of the project.

2. **#12 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea"** (Rong et al., 2026, *Remote Sensing*). Relevant on the method side: a YOLO11-based framework (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) for automated, large-scale extraction of ocean features from satellite imagery. The pattern — ML for automated, long-term satellite monitoring — transfers to detecting and tracking debris from space, which fits the lab's "Observing from space" cluster.

3. **#6 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026, Zenodo). Relevant as the forecasting/flow-field backbone: particle tracking for debris pathways needs realistic ocean currents, and a regional forecast system producing daily analyses is the kind of forcing data the tracking experiments would run against. (Note: I could only see the title and deposit details for this one — no abstract or method reading was available — so I'm ranking it on its role as a flow-field source rather than on its content.)

The other new papers on the slate (#5 LiDAR phytoplankton, #9 a comment, #11 multi-object tracking) are further afield from debris pathways.

## One funding opportunity to apply to

**#10 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC), NSF** — still open, deadline **2027-02-15**.

- **Why it fits:** OTIC supports unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science that enhance observational, experimental or analytical capabilities. A plastic-pathways project that develops new particle-tracking kernels, satellite-detection methods or a debris-forecasting tool is squarely "technology development that enhances analytical capabilities for the ocean science community" — and the lab's statement (ocean models + satellite observations + ML, handed to coastal managers) is a natural fit for the "broad applicability" bar.
- **The biggest doubt:** OTIC leans toward *instrumentation and technology development* rather than pure application or field study. The strongest case would frame the project around a reusable technical contribution (e.g., the beaching kernel or the satellite-detection framework) rather than a single regional study.
- **What I could not check:** the full eligibility rules (institution type, career stage, sub-award limits) and the budget ceiling aren't in what I can see, so confirm those against the NSF page before committing.

There's also a larger, more infrastructure-oriented option on the slate — **#3, the €50M EU "stronger Global Ocean Observing System" call** (deadline 2027-02-16) — but that is aimed at observing networks and GOOS governance at global scale, a heavier lift than a single project would typically carry. OTIC is the more realistic near-term target for this project.

If you'd like, I can pull the full text of #7 or #12 to dig into the methods, or look at who in the lab is best placed to lead an OTIC application.

Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.
